learn.b: R is a language made for working with data. You type a line in the console, press Enter, and R shows the result right away. R can be used as a calculator, with + - * / and ^ for powers. Anything after # is a comment and R ignores it.
Results print with a leading [1], which just means the first value on that line. Use print() to show a value from inside a script, and cat() to print plain text without the [1] or quotes.
The arrow <- stores a value under a name, like x <- 10. Read it as x gets 10. You can use = too, but R programmers prefer <-. Names are case sensitive, so score and Score are different.
Put a question mark before a function name, like ?mean, to open its help page. ls() lists the names you have created. R is vectorized and 1-based, which you will see in the next lessons.

o: Stores a value in a name

learn.b: A vector is an ordered list of values of the same type. c() combines values into a vector. The colon makes ranges, so 1:5 is 1 2 3 4 5. seq() makes sequences with a step, and rep() repeats values.
Math works on the whole vector at once, element by element. v * 2 doubles every number, and adding two vectors adds them pair by pair. You almost never need a loop for simple math in R.
length() counts items, sum() adds them, mean() gives the average, max() and min() find extremes, sort() orders them, and rev() reverses. These return a single value or a new vector.

If two vectors have different lengths, R repeats the shorter one to match. So c(1,2,3,4) + c(10,20) gives 11 22 13 24. If the lengths do not divide evenly you get a warning. Use paste() to join text vectors.

learn.b: R has numeric (like 3.5), integer (like 3L), character (text in quotes), and logical (TRUE or FALSE). class() tells you the type of a value. TRUE and FALSE are written in capital letters.
as.numeric(), as.character() and as.integer() change the type. as.numeric("12") gives 12. If a text cannot be converted you get NA with a warning. NA means a missing value, and is.na() tests for it.

A factor stores categories, like small, medium, large. Internally R stores numbers with labels called levels. Use factor() to create one and levels() to see the categories. Factors are used heavily in stats and plots.

Comparisons like >, <, ==, != return logical values. Combine them with & for and, | for or, and ! for not. Use == to compare, never a single = which assigns. TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0 in math, so sum() counts TRUEs.

learn.b: A data frame is a table where each column is a vector and all columns have the same length. Columns can have different types, like names and ages. It is the most important structure in R for data analysis.
learn.code:
df <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Bo"),
  age = c(12, 15)
)

learn.b: print(df) shows it, head(df) shows the first six rows, nrow() and ncol() give the size, and names() lists the columns. str() shows the structure and types. summary() gives quick statistics for each column.
Use the dollar sign to get a column: df$age. You can create a new column by assigning to a name that does not exist yet. The new column is computed for all rows at once.

read.csv("file.csv") loads a CSV file into a data frame, and write.csv() saves one. Add row.names = FALSE when saving to avoid an extra column. Built-in practice data sets like mtcars and iris are ready to use without importing.

qs.q: What is a data frame?
o: A table of columns of equal length

learn.b: Use v[2] to get the second element. R counts from 1, not 0. A negative index drops an item, so v[-1] is everything except the first. v[2:3] gets a range, and v[c(1,3)] gets chosen positions.
Put a condition inside the brackets to keep only matching values. v[v > 15] gives the values greater than 15. The condition makes a TRUE/FALSE vector and only the TRUE positions are kept.

A data frame has two dimensions: df[row, column]. Leave one empty to get all. df[1, ] is the first row, df[, 2] is the second column, and df[df$age > 12, ] keeps the rows where age is above 12. Do not forget the comma.
A list can hold different things, like a number, text and a vector. Use [[ ]] or $ to get an item out, and single [ ] to get a smaller list. For a named list, lst$name and lst[["name"]] both work.

qs.why: A negative index removes that position.

learn.b: A function packages code you can reuse. Use function() and assign it to a name. The last value computed is returned automatically, and return() can end it early. Call it with parentheses.
A function can take several arguments, separated by commas. Give an argument a default with an equals sign, and callers may skip it. You can pass arguments by name, which makes code easier to read.

Without return(), R gives back the last line. Writing return(x) is clearer in longer functions, or when you want to stop early. A function can return only one object, but that object can be a vector or a list.

Variables created inside a function exist only while it runs. They do not change variables outside, even with the same name. If you want a result, return it. Many built-in functions like sum, mean and paste work the same way.

learn.b: if runs code when a condition is TRUE. Use else if for more choices and else for everything left. The condition must be a single TRUE or FALSE, and curly braces hold the code.
A for loop repeats code for each item in a vector. The loop variable takes each value in turn. 1:3 makes a convenient range. Use it when you really need to repeat steps.
A while loop repeats as long as its condition is TRUE, so make sure something changes or it never ends. break leaves a loop early and next skips to the next round.
ifelse(test, yes, no) works on a whole vector at once, which is faster than a loop. Inside an if use && for and, and || for or, because they work on single values. Use & and | for vectors.

qs.why: for (i in x) loops over x.

qs.why: next skips a round, break ends the loop.

learn.b: The apply functions run a function over many items without writing a loop. The code is shorter and clearer. They take the data first and the function second.
lapply returns a list. sapply does the same job but simplifies the result into a vector when it can. You can pass a built-in function by name, like sapply(df, mean).
learn.code:
nums <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6)
lapply(nums, sum)
sapply(nums, sum)

learn.b: apply(m, 1, sum) runs sum on each row, and apply(m, 2, sum) runs it on each column. The second number is the margin: 1 for rows, 2 for columns.
learn.code:
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)
apply(m, 1, sum)
apply(m, 2, sum)

learn.b: tapply(values, groups, fun) applies a function to values split by group, such as the mean score per class. vapply is like sapply but you declare the output type, so it is safer in programs.

qs.q: What does sapply do?
o: Applies a function to each item and simplifies the result
qs.why: It returns a vector when possible.

learn.b: dplyr is a package that makes data wrangling easy. Install it once with install.packages("dplyr") and load it each session with library(dplyr). Its functions take a data frame first and return a new data frame, with readable verbs for each job.
filter() keeps rows that match a condition. select() keeps chosen columns. arrange() sorts rows, and desc() sorts from high to low. Column names are written without quotes or dollar signs.
learn.code:
filter(df, age > 12)
select(df, name, age)
arrange(df, desc(age))

learn.b: mutate() adds or changes columns. summarise() collapses many rows into one summary row, like a mean or count. n() counts rows in a group.
learn.code:
mutate(df, next_age = age + 1)
summarise(df, avg = mean(age))

learn.b: group_by() splits data into groups so summarise works per group. The pipe passes the left result into the next function, so steps read left to right. The classic pipe is %>% and the built-in one is |>.

learn.b: ggplot2 builds charts in layers. ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) sets the data and which columns go on which axis, and a plus sign adds layers like geom_point() for a scatter plot. Load it with library(ggplot2).

geom_point draws dots, geom_line draws lines, geom_col or geom_bar draws bars, and geom_histogram shows how values are spread. labs() adds a title and axis labels. aes(color = group) colors points by a column.

mean() is the average and median() is the middle value, which is less affected by outliers. sd() measures how spread out values are, and range(), min() and max() give the extremes. summary() prints several at once.
cor(x, y) gives correlation from -1 to 1. lm(y ~ x) fits a straight line, and summary() of the model shows the slope. The tilde means y depends on x. A t.test() compares the means of two groups.
learn.code:
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
coef(fit)
cor(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
